vignette:
# The Ejection

Marcus sits in the clinic waiting room with his hands folded in his lap, his posture rigid despite the comfortable chair. At fifty-six, he has the bearing of someone accustomed to discipline, though his jaw clenches periodically and his eyes dart toward the door. He's been a combat pilot for thirty-four years—F-16s mostly, though he transitioned to training younger pilots a decade ago. He tells himself that desk-adjacent work was supposed to feel safer.

Three years ago, during a routine training flight, his aircraft experienced catastrophic hydraulic failure at eight thousand feet. Marcus remembers the instrument panel lighting up like a Christmas tree, remembers the moment his hands moved through the emergency procedures with the automaticity of thousands of hours, remembers realizing none of it would matter. The ejection seat fired at 6,500 feet. He descended under parachute into a densely forested area, landing hard against a ridge. He fractured his left arm in two places and suffered a concussion. The physical injuries healed within months.

The other injuries didn't.

Now, sitting in his home office where he's transitioned to administrative work, Marcus finds himself unable to focus on spreadsheets for more than a few minutes. His mind keeps returning to that moment of weightlessness after ejection, the terrible silence when the engines cut out, the knowledge that his training and experience meant nothing against mechanical failure. He'll be reviewing pilot reports and suddenly his chest tightens, his breathing becomes shallow, and he's back in that cockpit, hands moving through procedures that won't save him.

His wife, Catherine, has noticed the changes. She finds him most mornings sitting in the kitchen at 4 a.m., having given up on sleep around 2 or 3. He doesn't snore anymore—he doesn't sleep deeply enough. When she touches his shoulder unexpectedly, he flinches violently, sometimes grabbing her wrist before recognition floods back. They haven't been intimate in nearly two years. He tells her it's not about her, and he means it, but his body has become hypervigilant to threat in ways that make vulnerability impossible.

Driving has become complicated. He avoids highways when possible, preferring surface streets where he can control speed and maintain awareness. When Catherine drives, he sits rigidly in the passenger seat, his foot pressing an imaginary brake, his eyes tracking every vehicle around them. He's never told her, but he scans rooflines and power lines when they're outside, calculating trajectories, assessing impact zones. The part of his brain trained to anticipate mechanical failure has become impossible to switch off.

Work has suffered. He's taken three extended leaves in the past two years, each time telling his commanding officer it was for minor health issues. The truth is that sitting in meetings about flight protocols, reviewing incident reports, watching younger pilots execute maneuvers—it all becomes too much. His chest constricts. His vision narrows. Last month, he excused himself from a briefing and spent forty minutes in the bathroom stall, breathing deliberately, reminding himself he was on the ground, that he was safe.

He hasn't flown since the accident. He tells people it's because of his administrative role, but the truth is more complicated. He's terrified of flying again, and equally terrified of never flying again. The thing that defined his adult life, the identity he's built across three decades, now feels like a threat. Marcus is caught between the person he was and the person the accident has made him—someone who startles at unexpected sounds, who can't watch aircraft footage, who lies awake cataloging all the ways systems fail.

He came to the clinic because Catherine finally said she couldn't watch him disappear anymore.
